chapter_text:
CHAPTER 28 — संस्कृतम् अन्याः भारतीयाः भाषाः च (SANSKRIT AND THE OTHER INDIAN LANGUAGES)

प्रस्तावना (Introduction)

भारतम् अनेकभाषाभूषितं राष्ट्रम् अस्ति। अत्र द्वाविंशतिः अनुसूचिताः भाषाः, शतशः च बोलयः सन्ति। तासु सर्वासु भाषासु संस्कृतस्य छाया स्पष्टं दृश्यते। India is a nation adorned with many languages — twenty-two scheduled languages and hundreds of dialects. Yet across this magnificent variety runs a golden thread: the presence of Sanskrit. In this lesson we study, at a linguistic level, HOW Sanskrit is related to the other Indian languages — as an ancestral source for some, as a generous lender of vocabulary to others, and as a shared treasury of word-roots for all. We shall see that the story is one of परस्परसमृद्धिः (mutual enrichment), not of hierarchy: Sanskrit gave abundantly to India's languages, and India's languages, in turn, kept Sanskrit alive, carried it into every region, and gave it words and vitality of their own.

1. भाषापरिवारौ — The Two Great Language Families

The major languages of India belong chiefly to two families. The भारतीय-आर्यभाषापरिवारः (Indo-Aryan family) includes Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Odia, Punjabi, Assamese, Nepali, Kashmiri, Sindhi and others. These languages are the modern descendants of Old Indo-Aryan — the language of the Vedas and of classical Sanskrit. They did not spring from Sanskrit overnight: the stream flowed through the middle stages of प्राकृतः (Prakrit) and अपभ्रंशः (Apabhramsha) before the modern languages took shape around the end of the first millennium CE. संस्कृतात् प्राकृतम्, प्राकृतात् अपभ्रंशः, अपभ्रंशात् च आधुनिकाः भाषाः जाताः।

The द्राविडभाषापरिवारः (Dravidian family) includes Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu and others. These languages are NOT daughters of Sanskrit — they form an independent family with its own ancient roots. Tamil, in particular, possesses a classical literature of great antiquity: the Sangam poems and the ancient grammar तोल्काप्पियम् (Tolkappiyam) testify to an independent literary tradition that flourished on its own strength. Yet centuries of shared life, scholarship, philosophy and devotion created a deep partnership between Sanskrit and the Dravidian languages, and an enormous Sanskrit vocabulary entered Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam especially, while Tamil too absorbed and adapted many Sanskrit words in its own manner.

2. तत्समशब्दाः तद्भवशब्दाश्च — Tatsama and Tadbhava Words

When we examine the vocabulary (शब्दराशिः) of Hindi, Bengali, Marathi and their sisters, we find four classes of words.

(क) तत्समशब्दाः — 'तस्य (संस्कृतस्य) समः इति तत्समः'. A tatsama word is used in exactly the same form as in Sanskrit. Examples in Hindi and most Indian languages: सूर्यः → सूर्य, अग्निः → अग्नि, पुस्तकम् → पुस्तक, कविः → कवि, माता, नदी, फलम् → फल, जलम् → जल, विद्या, धर्मः → धर्म। Bengali and Marathi are especially rich in tatsama words; formal and literary registers of nearly every Indian language draw freely on them.

(ख) तद्भवशब्दाः — 'तस्मात् (संस्कृतात्) भवः इति तद्भवः'. A tadbhava word is BORN FROM Sanskrit but has changed its form while travelling through Prakrit and Apabhramsha. Observe these classic pairs (संस्कृतम् → हिन्दी):
  • कर्म → काम (work)
  • हस्तः → हाथ (hand)
  • दुग्धम् → दूध (milk)
  • ग्रामः → गाँव (village)
  • अक्षि → आँख (eye)
  • कर्णः → कान (ear)
  • दन्तः → दाँत (tooth)
  • चन्द्रः → चाँद (moon)
  • सप्त → सात (seven)
  • शतम् → सौ (hundred)
  • अग्निः → आग (fire)
  • क्षेत्रम् → खेत (field)
  • घृतम् → घी (clarified butter)
  • सर्पः → साँप (snake)
  • हस्ती (हस्तिन्) → हाथी (elephant)
  • रात्रिः → रात (night)
Notice the regular sound changes: conjunct consonants simplify (क्ष → ख, as in क्षेत्र → खेत), aspirates and vowels soften (दुग्ध → दूध), and a lost nasal often survives as a candrabindu (चन्द्र → चाँद, ग्राम → गाँव). Such regular correspondences are the delight of linguists — they show that these words were not casually borrowed but organically inherited.

(ग) देशजशब्दाः — words born of the local soil, e.g. Hindi लोटा, पगड़ी। (घ) विदेशजशब्दाः — words borrowed from foreign languages, e.g. स्कूल (English), क़लम (Arabic), बाज़ार (Persian)। A living language welcomes all four classes; the tatsama–tadbhava pair, however, is the special bond that ties the Indo-Aryan languages to Sanskrit.

3. द्राविडभाषाः संस्कृतं च — Sanskrit and the Dravidian Languages

Though Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Tamil belong to a different family, their vocabularies carry a vast treasure of Sanskrit words, above all in the domains of philosophy, religion, science, law and literature. In Telugu and Kannada, learned vocabulary is very largely Sanskritic; their classical poets composed under the direct inspiration of the Sanskrit kavya tradition. Malayalam developed a celebrated literary style called मणिप्रवालम् (Manipravalam) — literally 'gems and coral' — in which Sanskrit and Malayalam words are strung together on one thread like a necklace of rubies and coral, a beautiful emblem of linguistic partnership. Tamil, while preserving its independent classical genius, also received Sanskrit words (often adapting them to its own phonology) and gave to the common Indian stock in return: linguists cite words such as मुरजः (a kind of drum) and कुटी (hut) as possible Dravidian contributions absorbed by Sanskrit itself. The exchange, again, was mutual — संस्कृतं ददाति, गृह्णाति च।

4. लिपीनाम् एकता — The Shared Origin of Indian Scripts

The unity of Indian languages appears not only in words but in writing. Almost all the scripts of India descend from one ancient mother: ब्राह्मीलिपिः (the Brahmi script), seen most famously in the rock and pillar inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka (circa third century BCE). From Brahmi, over the centuries, evolved देवनागरी (used for Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi, Nepali), and the Bengali-Assamese, Gujarati, Gurmukhi (Punjabi), Odia, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Tamil scripts (the last through Tamil-Brahmi). Another ancient script, खरोष्ठी (Kharoshthi), written from right to left in the north-west, died out and left no descendants. All Brahmi-born scripts share two deep features: (1) they are 'abugidas' — each consonant letter carries an inherent अ, and other vowels are shown by matras; (2) they arrange the alphabet in the same scientific phonetic order — क ख ग घ ङ … — inherited from the Sanskrit grammarians' analysis of sounds. A student who knows Devanagari thus already understands the inner logic of the Telugu or Kannada script, even before learning its shapes.

5. आधुनिकाः पारिभाषिकशब्दाः — Sanskrit and Modern Technical Coinage

When the modern age demanded new words for new things, India's languages turned together to Sanskrit. From Sanskrit roots (धातवः), prefixes (उपसर्गाः) and suffixes (प्रत्ययाः), thousands of precise technical terms were coined and adopted across languages: दूरदर्शनम् (television — 'seeing from afar'), आकाशवाणी (radio — 'voice from the sky'), दूरभाषः (telephone), संगणकः (computer), विश्वविद्यालयः (university), महाविद्यालयः (college), प्रधानमन्त्री (prime minister), विज्ञानम् (science), प्रौद्योगिकी (technology), विद्युत् (electricity), शल्यचिकित्सा (surgery)। Because Sanskrit's word-building machinery is systematic — a root like दृश् (to see) yields दर्शनम्, दूरदर्शनम्, दर्शकः, प्रदर्शनम् — one coinage is instantly intelligible from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. The same Sanskrit word often serves Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Telugu and Kannada alike, knitting the languages together in the vocabulary of law, administration, science and education. Sanskrit's gifts even crossed the seas: languages of Southeast Asia such as Indonesian and Thai still carry hundreds of Sanskrit-origin words (Indonesian 'bahasa' itself is भाषा).

6. परस्परसमृद्धिः — Mutual Enrichment, Not Hierarchy

The correct picture, then, is not a pyramid with Sanskrit ruling from the top, but a family gathering around a shared treasury. Sanskrit is an ancestral source for the Indo-Aryan languages and a generous partner of the Dravidian languages; every modern language, in turn, preserved, popularised and enriched that inheritance in its own soil. Regional languages carried Sanskrit's ideas to every home through saints and poets; they lent Sanskrit fresh words; and their scripts, songs and scholarship kept the classical language a living presence. सर्वाः भारतीयाः भाषाः भगिन्यः इव परस्परं पोषयन्ति। All Indian languages, like sisters, nourish one another.

7. व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the Lesson

(A) सन्धिः। दीर्घसन्धिः: विद्या + आलयः = विद्यालयः (आ + आ = आ); महा + आत्मा = महात्मा। गुणसन्धिः: सूर्य + उदयः = सूर्योदयः (अ + उ = ओ); गण + ईशः = गणेशः (अ + ई = ए)। व्यञ्जनसन्धिः: तत् + भवः = तद्भवः — the त् becomes द् before the voiced भ्; likewise वाक् + ईशः = वागीशः। सन्धिविच्छेदः (splitting) is the reverse skill: विश्वविद्यालयः = विश्व + विद्या + आलयः।

(B) समासः। तत्पुरुषः: राजपुरुषः = राज्ञः पुरुषः (the king's man); कर्मधारयः: नीलोत्पलम् = नीलम् उत्पलम् (blue lotus); द्वन्द्वः: रामलक्ष्मणौ = रामः च लक्ष्मणः च; बहुव्रीहिः: पीताम्बरः = पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः (he whose garment is yellow — Vishnu)। Modern coinages are mostly तत्पुरुष/कर्मधारय compounds: दूरदर्शनम् = दूरात् दर्शनम्।

(C) विभक्तिः। The feminine आकारान्त noun भाषा declines: प्रथमा भाषा, द्वितीया भाषाम्, तृतीया भाषया (by the language), चतुर्थी भाषायै, पञ्चमी भाषायाः, षष्ठी भाषायाः, सप्तमी भाषायाम् (in the language)। In the lesson: संस्कृतस्य (षष्ठी, 'of Sanskrit'), भाषासु (सप्तमी बहुवचनम्, 'among the languages'), संस्कृतात् (पञ्चमी, 'from Sanskrit')।

(D) शब्दनिर्माणम्। From धातु दृश् with उपसर्ग and प्रत्यय: दर्शनम्, प्रदर्शनम्, दूरदर्शनम्; from गण् (to count): गणना, गणकः, संगणकः। This root-based derivation is exactly why Sanskrit remains India's common mint for new words.

सारांशः (Summary)

In this chapter you learned that India's languages fall chiefly into the Indo-Aryan family (descended from Sanskrit through Prakrit and Apabhramsha) and the Dravidian family (independent in origin, deeply enriched by partnership with Sanskrit). You studied the four classes of vocabulary — तत्सम, तद्भव, देशज, विदेशज — with classic tadbhava derivations such as कर्म → काम, हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध; the vast Sanskrit word-stock of Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam and the Manipravalam style; Tamil's independent classical greatness; the descent of nearly all Indian scripts from Ashokan Brahmi; and Sanskrit's modern role as the shared mint of technical terms like दूरदर्शनम् and संगणकः। Above all, you learned to see the relation rightly: mutual enrichment among sister languages gathered around a common treasury — वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम्, भाषाक्षेत्रे अपि।

key_takeaways: India's major languages belong to two families: Indo-Aryan (descended from Sanskrit via Prakrit and Apabhramsha) and Dravidian (independent in origin, deeply enriched by partnership with Sanskrit).
तत्सम words are used unchanged from Sanskrit (सूर्य, पुस्तक); तद्भव words evolved from Sanskrit with regular sound changes (हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध, ग्राम → गाँव).
Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam carry vast Sanskrit vocabularies; Malayalam's मणिप्रवालम् style blends the two literatures like gems and coral.
Tamil possesses an independent ancient classical tradition (Sangam, Tolkappiyam); borrowing between Sanskrit and Dravidian languages was mutual.
Nearly all Indian scripts descend from Ashokan Brahmi (3rd century BCE) and share the abugida principle and the phonetic order क ख ग घ...
Sanskrit is India's shared mint for modern technical terms — दूरदर्शनम्, आकाशवाणी, संगणकः, विश्वविद्यालयः — thanks to its root-based derivational system.
The right picture of the relation is mutual enrichment among sister languages gathered around a shared treasury, not a hierarchy.

glossary.definition: 'तस्य समः' — a word used in an Indian language in exactly the same form as in Sanskrit, e.g. सूर्य, अग्नि, पुस्तक, विद्या.
'तस्मात् भवः' — a word born from Sanskrit but changed in form while passing through Prakrit and Apabhramsha, e.g. हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध.
A word native to the local soil, belonging to neither Sanskrit nor a foreign source, e.g. Hindi लोटा, पगड़ी.
A word borrowed from a foreign language, e.g. स्कूल (English), बाज़ार (Persian), क़लम (Arabic).
The Middle Indo-Aryan speech stage between Sanskrit and Apabhramsha, through which tadbhava words evolved.
The late Middle Indo-Aryan stage from which the modern Indo-Aryan languages such as Hindi, Marathi and Bengali took shape.
The Dravidian language family — Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu — independent in origin and a deep partner of Sanskrit.
'Gems and coral' — the celebrated Kerala literary style that strings Sanskrit and Malayalam words together on one thread.
The ancient grammar of Tamil, a monument of Tamil's independent classical tradition alongside the Sangam poems.
The ancient mother script of India, seen in Ashoka's inscriptions (c. 3rd century BCE), from which most Indian scripts descend.
An ancient right-to-left script of north-west India, contemporary with Brahmi, which died out leaving no descendant scripts.
The Brahmi-descended script used for Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali; an abugida whose consonants carry an inherent अ.
A technical term coined for a precise modern concept, typically minted from Sanskrit roots, e.g. दूरदर्शनम्, संगणकः, विद्युत्.
A Sanskrit verbal root, the seed of word derivation — दृश् (see) yields दर्शनम् and दूरदर्शनम्; गण् (count) yields संगणकः.
Mutual enrichment — the chapter's central idea that Sanskrit and the Indian languages nourished one another like sisters, without hierarchy.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — संस्कृतम् अन्याः भारतीयाः भाषाः च (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 28)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give your explanations in English. Refer to the tatsama-tadbhava lists, the script history and the grammar section of the lesson where needed.

questions.question: Define तत्सम and तद्भव words with their Sanskrit etymologies, and give two examples of each from Hindi.
questions.answer: A तत्सम word (तस्य समः = 'same as it') is used in exactly the same form as in Sanskrit, e.g. सूर्य, पुस्तक (also अग्नि, विद्या). A तद्भव word (तस्मात् भवः = 'born from it') evolved from Sanskrit through Prakrit and Apabhramsha with a change of form, e.g. हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध.
questions.explanation: The etymologies तस्य समः and तस्मात् भवः themselves explain the two classes.

questions.question: Give the Hindi tadbhava form of each Sanskrit word: कर्म, ग्रामः, अक्षि, चन्द्रः.
questions.answer: कर्म → काम; ग्रामः → गाँव; अक्षि → आँख; चन्द्रः → चाँद.
questions.explanation: Note the regular changes: cluster simplification and the nasal surviving as candrabindu (गाँव, आँख, चाँद).

questions.question: What is the ब्राह्मी script, and why is it called the mother of Indian scripts?
questions.answer: Brahmi is the ancient Indian script seen most famously in Emperor Ashoka's rock and pillar inscriptions (about the 3rd century BCE). It is called the mother of Indian scripts because almost all later Indian scripts — Devanagari, Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Odia, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Tamil (via Tamil-Brahmi) — evolved from it over the centuries.
questions.explanation: Kharoshthi, by contrast, died out without descendants.

questions.question: Do the सन्धिविच्छेद (split) and name the sandhi: (a) विद्यालयः (b) सूर्योदयः.
questions.answer: (a) विद्यालयः = विद्या + आलयः (आ + आ = आ, दीर्घसन्धिः). (b) सूर्योदयः = सूर्य + उदयः (अ + उ = ओ, गुणसन्धिः).
questions.explanation: Splitting a joined form back into its parts is सन्धिविच्छेद.

questions.question: Explain how दूरदर्शनम् and आकाशवाणी were coined, and what they mean.
questions.answer: दूरदर्शनम् = दूर (far) + दर्शनम् (seeing, from the root दृश्) — 'seeing from afar', the coined term for television. आकाशवाणी = आकाश (sky) + वाणी (voice) — 'voice from the sky', the coined term for radio. Both are modern technical terms minted from Sanskrit roots and shared across Indian languages.
questions.explanation: Such coinages show Sanskrit's role as the common mint of technical vocabulary.

questions.question: "The relation between Sanskrit and the other Indian languages is one of mutual enrichment, not hierarchy." Evaluate this statement with evidence from vocabulary, scripts and modern coinage.
questions.answer: The statement is well supported. (1) Vocabulary: Sanskrit gave the Indo-Aryan languages their inherited word-stock (tadbhava words like हस्त → हाथ) and a vast tatsama treasury used by Bengali, Marathi, Hindi and others; the Dravidian languages too absorbed enormous Sanskrit vocabulary in scholarship and religion. But the traffic was two-way — regional languages gave Sanskrit fresh words (linguists cite possible Dravidian contributions such as मुरज and कुटी), and the regional literatures kept Sanskrit's ideas alive in every home. (2) Scripts: nearly all Indian scripts, north and south, descend from one mother, Brahmi, and share the abugida principle and phonetic order — a common inheritance rather than an imposition. (3) Coinage: when modern terms were needed, all languages drew together on Sanskrit roots (दूरदर्शनम्, संगणकः, विश्वविद्यालयः), and the same coinages serve Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and Kannada alike. Meanwhile Tamil's independent classical tradition (Sangam, Tolkappiyam) shows that the family has more than one ancient treasure. The picture is thus a family gathered around shared treasuries — sisters nourishing one another — not a pyramid with Sanskrit ruling from the top.
questions.explanation: A full answer cites both directions of giving: Sanskrit's gifts to the languages, and the languages' preservation and enrichment of Sanskrit.

questions.question: Describe the partnership between Sanskrit and the Dravidian languages. Your answer should mention Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam (मणिप्रवालम्) and Tamil's classical tradition.
questions.answer: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to the independent Dravidian family — they are partners of Sanskrit, not its daughters. Yet centuries of shared scholarship, philosophy and devotion built a deep partnership. Telugu and Kannada carry a very large Sanskrit vocabulary, especially in learned domains, and their classical poets wrote under the inspiration of the Sanskrit kavya tradition. Malayalam developed the celebrated मणिप्रवालम् ('gems and coral') style, stringing Sanskrit and Malayalam words together like a necklace of rubies and coral. Tamil preserved its independent classical genius — the Sangam poems and the ancient grammar तोल्काप्पियम् — while also adapting Sanskrit words to its own phonology; and borrowing went both ways, for Sanskrit itself is held to have absorbed words of Dravidian origin. The partnership is thus one of mutual respect and mutual enrichment.
questions.explanation: The answer must respect Tamil's independent classical status while describing the shared Sanskrit vocabulary of the southern languages.

questions.question: Name the two major language families of India and give two member languages of each. Through which two intermediate stages did the modern Indo-Aryan languages evolve from Sanskrit?
questions.answer: The Indo-Aryan family (e.g. Hindi and Bengali; also Marathi, Gujarati, Odia, Punjabi) and the Dravidian family (e.g. Tamil and Telugu; also Kannada, Malayalam). The modern Indo-Aryan languages evolved from Sanskrit (Old Indo-Aryan) through the intermediate stages of प्राकृत (Prakrit) and अपभ्रंश (Apabhramsha).
questions.explanation: संस्कृतात् प्राकृतम्, प्राकृतात् अपभ्रंशः, अपभ्रंशात् आधुनिकाः भाषाः।

questions.question: Classify each Hindi word as तत्सम or तद्भव: पुस्तक, दाँत, अग्नि, खेत.
questions.answer: पुस्तक — तत्सम (same as Sanskrit पुस्तकम्). दाँत — तद्भव (from दन्तः). अग्नि — तत्सम (same as अग्निः). खेत — तद्भव (from क्षेत्रम्, with क्ष → ख).
questions.explanation: Unchanged forms are tatsama; changed, inherited forms are tadbhava.

questions.question: Translate into English: "सर्वाः भारतीयाः भाषाः भगिन्यः इव परस्परं पोषयन्ति। संस्कृतं तासां शब्दभाण्डारं वर्धयति।"
questions.answer: "All Indian languages nourish one another like sisters. Sanskrit increases (enriches) their treasury of words." भगिन्यः = sisters; परस्परम् = one another; पोषयन्ति = they nourish; शब्दभाण्डारम् = word-treasury; वर्धयति = increases.
questions.explanation: The two sentences state the chapter's central thesis of sisterly mutual enrichment.

questions.question: In this chapter, Sanskrit's relation to the other Indian languages is best described as
options: a source and enricher of their vocabulary
a foreign language unrelated to them
questions.answer: a source and enricher of their vocabulary
questions.explanation: Sanskrit is an ancestral source for Indo-Aryan languages and a generous lender of vocabulary to all.

questions.question: Hindi, Marathi, Bengali and Gujarati belong to which language family?
questions.explanation: They are modern descendants of Old Indo-Aryan (the language of the Vedas and classical Sanskrit).

questions.question: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to which language family?
questions.explanation: The Dravidian family is an independent family with its own ancient roots.

questions.question: The modern Indo-Aryan languages evolved from Sanskrit through which intermediate stages?
questions.explanation: संस्कृतात् प्राकृतम्, प्राकृतात् अपभ्रंशः, अपभ्रंशात् आधुनिकाः भाषाः।

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an Indo-Aryan language?
questions.explanation: Kannada is a Dravidian language; the other three are Indo-Aryan.

questions.question: For modern languages like Hindi and Bengali, Sanskrit is best described as
options: an ancestral source of their inherited vocabulary
a language they replaced by force
a dialect that arose from Hindi
questions.answer: an ancestral source of their inherited vocabulary
questions.explanation: The Indo-Aryan languages descend from Old Indo-Aryan through Prakrit and Apabhramsha.

questions.question: The chief way Sanskrit enriched ALL Indian languages, of both families, is through
options: its treasury of words and word-roots (शब्दराशिः)
questions.answer: its treasury of words and word-roots (शब्दराशिः)
questions.explanation: Vocabulary — tatsama, tadbhava and technical coinages — is the great shared inheritance.

questions.question: The chapter's view of the relation among Indian languages is best summarised as
options: a pyramid with Sanskrit ruling from the top
one-way borrowing from regional languages into Sanskrit
questions.explanation: परस्परसमृद्धिः — the languages nourish one another like sisters; there is no hierarchy.

questions.question: How did the regional languages, in turn, serve Sanskrit?
options: They kept it alive, carried its ideas to every region and lent it words
They had no effect on Sanskrit at all
They only translated foreign books into Sanskrit
They replaced its script with Kharoshthi
questions.answer: They kept it alive, carried its ideas to every region and lent it words
questions.explanation: Enrichment was mutual: the regional languages preserved, popularised and fed the classical language.

questions.question: A तत्सम word is one that is
options: used in the same form as in Sanskrit
questions.answer: used in the same form as in Sanskrit
questions.explanation: तस्य समः इति तत्समः — 'same as it (Sanskrit)'.

questions.question: A तद्भव word is one that is
options: evolved from Sanskrit with a change of form
questions.answer: evolved from Sanskrit with a change of form
questions.explanation: तस्मात् भवः इति तद्भवः — 'born from it (Sanskrit)', changed via Prakrit and Apabhramsha.

questions.question: The etymology of तत्सम is
questions.explanation: तत् (that, i.e. Sanskrit) + सम (same) = तत्सम.

questions.question: Tadbhava words reached Hindi from Sanskrit through
options: direct borrowing in the modern period
questions.explanation: They were organically inherited through the Middle Indo-Aryan stages, not casually borrowed.

questions.question: In Hindi, the word सूर्य is
questions.explanation: It keeps the same form as Sanskrit सूर्यः, so it is tatsama.

questions.question: In Hindi, the word दूध is
questions.explanation: दूध evolved from Sanskrit दुग्धम् with a change of form — hence tadbhava.

questions.question: A देशज word is one that
options: is born of the local soil, e.g. लोटा
questions.answer: is born of the local soil, e.g. लोटा
questions.explanation: देशज = 'born in the region' — native words belonging to neither Sanskrit nor a foreign source.

questions.question: Which of these Hindi words is विदेशज (a foreign loan)?
questions.explanation: स्कूल is from English 'school'; सूर्य is tatsama, हाथ and आग are tadbhava.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched as Sanskrit → Hindi tadbhava?
questions.explanation: हस्त (hand) became हाथ through the Prakrit stage — a classic tadbhava.

questions.question: Which Indian languages are noted in the lesson as especially rich in tatsama words?
questions.explanation: Bengali and Marathi make especially heavy use of unchanged Sanskrit (tatsama) vocabulary.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit कर्म is
questions.explanation: कर्म (work) → काम, via the Prakrit form कम्म.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit दुग्धम् is
questions.explanation: दुग्ध → दूध: the conjunct ग्ध simplifies and the vowel lengthens.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit ग्रामः is
questions.explanation: ग्राम → गाँव: the cluster simplifies and the nasal survives as candrabindu.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit अक्षि (eye) is
questions.explanation: अक्षि → आँख: क्ष becomes ख and a nasal appears as candrabindu.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit चन्द्रः is
questions.explanation: चन्द्र → चाँद: the cluster न्द्र simplifies and the nasal remains as candrabindu.

questions.question: The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit सप्त (seven) is
questions.explanation: सप्त → सात: the cluster प्त simplifies to त with a lengthened vowel.

questions.question: The Hindi word हाथी (elephant) comes from which Sanskrit word?
questions.explanation: हस्तिन् 'the one with a hand (trunk)' → हाथी, just as हस्त → हाथ.

questions.question: The Hindi word कान (ear) comes from which Sanskrit word?
questions.explanation: कर्ण → कान: the cluster र्ण simplifies to न.

questions.question: The Hindi word खेत (field) comes from which Sanskrit word?
questions.explanation: क्षेत्र → खेत: the conjunct क्ष regularly becomes ख in tadbhava words.

questions.question: Which of the following Hindi words is a तद्भव word?
questions.explanation: आग evolved from अग्निः (via Prakrit अग्गि); the other three are unchanged tatsama forms.

questions.question: In which Dravidian languages is learned vocabulary especially heavily Sanskritic?
questions.explanation: These three absorbed a vast Sanskrit vocabulary, above all in philosophy, religion, science and literature.

questions.question: मणिप्रवालम् (Manipravalam) refers to
options: a Kerala literary style blending Sanskrit and Malayalam
questions.answer: a Kerala literary style blending Sanskrit and Malayalam
questions.explanation: Sanskrit and Malayalam words are strung together on one thread like a necklace.

questions.question: The word मणिप्रवाल literally means
questions.explanation: मणि (gem/ruby) + प्रवाल (coral) — the two literatures strung like a mixed necklace.

questions.question: The Sangam poems show that Tamil possesses
options: no literature before the modern period
questions.explanation: Tamil's classical literature flourished on its own strength, alongside its partnership with Sanskrit.

questions.question: तोल्काप्पियम् (Tolkappiyam) is
questions.explanation: Tolkappiyam is a monument of Tamil's independent classical tradition.

questions.question: Sanskrit words entered the Dravidian languages especially in the domains of
options: philosophy, religion, science, law and literature
questions.answer: philosophy, religion, science, law and literature
questions.explanation: Learned and scholarly domains drew most heavily on the Sanskrit word-treasury.

questions.question: Which words do linguists cite as possible Dravidian contributions absorbed by Sanskrit?
questions.explanation: Borrowing was mutual — Sanskrit too is held to have absorbed words of Dravidian origin.

questions.question: The classical poets of early Telugu and Kannada composed under the inspiration of
questions.explanation: Early Telugu and Kannada court literature drew directly on Sanskrit poetics and themes.

questions.question: How did Tamil generally treat the Sanskrit words it received?
options: It adapted them to its own phonology
It refused all contact with them
It wrote them only in Devanagari
It used them without any change ever
questions.answer: It adapted them to its own phonology
questions.explanation: Tamil absorbed Sanskrit words in its own manner while preserving its classical genius.

questions.question: The correct description of the Dravidian languages' relation to Sanskrit is
options: partners of Sanskrit, not its daughters
questions.answer: partners of Sanskrit, not its daughters
questions.explanation: They form an independent family, deeply enriched by centuries of partnership with Sanskrit.

questions.question: The mother script from which most Indian scripts descend is
questions.explanation: Brahmi is the ancient ancestor of nearly all Indian scripts, north and south.

questions.question: The Brahmi script is seen most famously in the inscriptions of
questions.explanation: Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts (c. 3rd century BCE) are the most famous Brahmi inscriptions.

questions.question: Devanagari is used to write which set of languages?
questions.explanation: Devanagari, itself a daughter of Brahmi, serves Sanskrit and several modern languages.

questions.question: The खरोष्ठी (Kharoshthi) script was written
questions.explanation: Kharoshthi, used in the north-west, ran right to left and died out without descendants.

questions.question: Brahmi-derived scripts are called 'abugidas' because
options: each consonant letter carries an inherent अ
they have no vowel signs at all
each letter stands for a whole word
they are written right to left
questions.answer: each consonant letter carries an inherent अ
questions.explanation: Other vowels are shown by matras attached to the consonant.

questions.question: Which of the following scripts descend from Brahmi?
options: Bengali, Telugu and Kannada — all of these
questions.answer: Bengali, Telugu and Kannada — all of these
questions.explanation: Almost all Indian scripts, northern and southern alike, evolved from Brahmi.

questions.question: The Tamil script descends from
questions.explanation: Tamil's script evolved from the southern (Tamil) variety of Brahmi.

questions.question: The Gurmukhi script is used to write
questions.explanation: Gurmukhi, a Brahmi descendant, is the script of Punjabi.

questions.question: A structural feature shared by all Brahmi-born scripts is
options: the same scientific phonetic order क ख ग घ ङ...
identical letter shapes in every language
questions.answer: the same scientific phonetic order क ख ग घ ङ...
questions.explanation: The alphabet order inherited from the Sanskrit grammarians' analysis of sounds is common to all.

questions.question: Ashoka's Brahmi inscriptions date to approximately
questions.explanation: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka's edicts belong to about the third century before the common era.

questions.question: दूरदर्शनम् (television) is formed from
questions.explanation: दर्शनम् comes from the root दृश् 'to see'; दूरदर्शनम् = seeing from a distance.

questions.question: आकाशवाणी, the coined name for radio, literally means
questions.explanation: आकाश (sky) + वाणी (voice/speech).

questions.question: The Sanskrit-based coinage for 'university' is
questions.explanation: विश्व + विद्या + आलय — the abode of universal learning; महाविद्यालयः is 'college'.

questions.question: The Sanskrit-based coinage for 'computer' is
questions.explanation: From the root गण् 'to count': गणना, गणकः, संगणकः.

questions.question: When Indian languages need new technical terms, they most commonly coin them from
questions.explanation: Sanskrit's धातु-उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय system is the shared mint of technical vocabulary.

questions.question: The Sanskrit-based coinage दूरभाषः stands for
questions.explanation: दूर (far) + भाष (speech) — speaking from afar.

questions.question: Why is Sanskrit especially well suited to coining new technical terms?
options: Its systematic root-prefix-suffix derivation makes coinages precise and transparent
It has no grammar rules to follow
It is the only language with a script
Its words are always shorter than English words
questions.answer: Its systematic root-prefix-suffix derivation makes coinages precise and transparent
questions.explanation: From one root like दृश् flow दर्शनम्, प्रदर्शनम्, दूरदर्शनम्, दर्शकः — each self-explaining.

questions.question: The word प्रधानमन्त्री is built from प्रधान + मन्त्री, meaning
questions.explanation: The same Sanskrit coinage serves administration across many Indian languages.

questions.question: Sanskrit-origin words also live on outside India — for example, Indonesian 'bahasa' comes from
questions.explanation: Languages of Southeast Asia such as Indonesian and Thai carry hundreds of Sanskrit-origin words.

questions.question: विद्या + आलयः = विद्यालयः is an example of which sandhi?
questions.explanation: आ + आ merge into a single long आ — the दीर्घ (lengthening) sandhi.

questions.question: सूर्य + उदयः = सूर्योदयः is an example of which sandhi?
questions.explanation: अ + उ = ओ, the guna combination.

questions.question: गण + ईशः = गणेशः shows which vowel combination?
questions.explanation: अ followed by ई yields ए by guna sandhi.

questions.question: In तत् + भवः = तद्भवः, the त् becomes द् because of
options: consonant (व्यञ्जन) sandhi before a voiced sound
questions.answer: consonant (व्यञ्जन) sandhi before a voiced sound
questions.explanation: Before the voiced भ्, the unvoiced त् is voiced to द् — the very name तद्भव embodies a sandhi rule.

questions.question: The सन्धिविच्छेद of विश्वविद्यालयः is
questions.explanation: विद्या + आलयः joins by दीर्घ sandhi; विश्व is prefixed to the compound.

questions.question: राजपुरुषः (= राज्ञः पुरुषः, the king's man) is which samasa?
questions.explanation: The first member stands in a case relation (षष्ठी) to the second — a tatpurusha compound.

questions.question: रामलक्ष्मणौ (= रामः च लक्ष्मणः च) is which samasa?
questions.explanation: Two members joined with the sense of 'and' form a dvandva compound.

questions.question: पीताम्बरः (= पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः, 'he whose garment is yellow') is which samasa?
questions.explanation: The compound denotes someone OUTSIDE its members (Vishnu), the mark of bahuvrihi.

questions.question: The तृतीया (instrumental) singular of भाषा is
questions.explanation: भाषा declines: भाषा, भाषाम्, भाषया ('by the language'), भाषायै, भाषायाः, भाषायाः, भाषायाम्.

questions.question: भाषायाम् ('in the language') is which vibhakti?
questions.explanation: The locative (सप्तमी) singular of भाषा is भाषायाम्.

questions.question: Which fact best supports the claim of MUTUAL enrichment between Sanskrit and the regional languages?
options: Sanskrit itself absorbed regional words while lending its own
Sanskrit never borrowed a single word
regional languages have no Sanskrit words
all Indian languages use the Roman script
questions.answer: Sanskrit itself absorbed regional words while lending its own
questions.explanation: Two-way borrowing is the strongest evidence that the exchange was mutual, not one-way.

questions.question: A student claims: 'Tamil is a daughter of Sanskrit.' The correct assessment is
options: False — Tamil is Dravidian with an independent origin, though enriched by contact with Sanskrit
True — all Indian languages descend from Sanskrit
questions.answer: False — Tamil is Dravidian with an independent origin, though enriched by contact with Sanskrit
questions.explanation: Tamil belongs to the independent Dravidian family and has its own ancient classical tradition.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the message of this chapter?
options: Sanskrit is a shared treasury that enriched, and was enriched by, the Indian languages
Indian languages have nothing in common
only Hindi is related to Sanskrit
questions.answer: Sanskrit is a shared treasury that enriched, and was enriched by, the Indian languages
questions.explanation: The family gathers around a common treasury — sisters nourishing one another.

questions.question: If one new scientific term must serve many Indian languages at once, the chapter suggests coining it from
options: Sanskrit roots, so it is intelligible across languages
a different source for every language
questions.answer: Sanskrit roots, so it is intelligible across languages
questions.explanation: One Sanskrit coinage — like दूरदर्शनम् — is instantly understood from Kashmir to Kanyakumari.

questions.question: The sentence 'संस्कृतं भारतीयभाषाणां शब्दभाण्डारं वर्धयति' means
options: Sanskrit increases the word-treasury of the Indian languages
Sanskrit closes the treasury of Indian languages
Sanskrit counts the letters of Indian scripts
questions.answer: Sanskrit increases the word-treasury of the Indian languages
questions.explanation: शब्दभाण्डारम् = treasury of words; वर्धयति = increases/enriches.

questions.question: The underlying unity of the Indian languages is visible in
options: shared vocabulary, shared script origin and shared technical coinage — all of these
questions.answer: shared vocabulary, shared script origin and shared technical coinage — all of these
questions.explanation: Words (tatsama/tadbhava), Brahmi-born scripts and Sanskrit-based coinages all bind the family together.

questions.question: Why is 'hierarchy' the WRONG frame for the relation among Indian languages?
options: Because each language, classical or modern, serves its people and enriches the others
Because Sanskrit is superior to all others
Because regional languages are superior to Sanskrit
questions.answer: Because each language, classical or modern, serves its people and enriches the others
questions.explanation: The chapter replaces the pyramid image with that of sisters around a shared treasury.

questions.question: All Indian languages, including Tamil, are direct daughters of Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: The Dravidian languages, including Tamil, form an independent family; only the Indo-Aryan languages descend from Sanskrit.

questions.question: A तत्सम word is used in the same form as in Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: तस्य समः — e.g. सूर्य, पुस्तक, विद्या are unchanged Sanskrit forms.

questions.question: Tadbhava words entered Hindi directly from Sanskrit without any intermediate stage.
questions.explanation: They evolved through the Prakrit and Apabhramsha stages.

questions.question: हाथ is the tadbhava form of Sanskrit हस्तः.
questions.explanation: हस्त → हाथ is a classic tadbhava derivation.

questions.question: The Manipravalam style of Kerala blends Sanskrit with Malayalam.
questions.explanation: मणिप्रवालम् ('gems and coral') strings the two languages together in one literary style.

questions.question: Kharoshthi is the ancestor of the Devanagari script.
questions.explanation: Devanagari descends from Brahmi; Kharoshthi died out without descendants.

questions.question: The Brahmi inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka date to about the 3rd century BCE.
questions.explanation: Ashoka's Mauryan-era rock and pillar edicts are the most famous early Brahmi records.

questions.question: दूरदर्शनम् is a modern coinage from Sanskrit roots meaning 'television'.
questions.explanation: दूर + दर्शन (root दृश्) = 'seeing from afar'.

questions.question: सूर्योदयः (सूर्य + उदयः) is an example of दीर्घ sandhi.
questions.explanation: अ + उ = ओ is गुण sandhi, not दीर्घ.

questions.question: Borrowing between Sanskrit and the other Indian languages went in one direction only.
questions.explanation: The exchange was mutual: Sanskrit lent vast vocabulary and also absorbed regional words.

questions.question: संस्कृतस्य 'दुग्धम्' इत्यस्य हिन्दीभाषायां तद्भवरूपम् ____ इति। (The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit दुग्धम् is ____.)
questions.explanation: दुग्ध → दूध — the conjunct simplifies and the vowel lengthens.

questions.question: संस्कृतस्य 'ग्रामः' इत्यस्य हिन्दीभाषायां तद्भवरूपम् ____ इति। (The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit ग्रामः is ____.)
questions.explanation: ग्राम → गाँव, with the nasal surviving as candrabindu.

questions.question: संस्कृतस्य 'कर्म' इत्यस्य हिन्दीभाषायां तद्भवरूपम् ____ इति। (The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit कर्म is ____.)
questions.explanation: कर्म → काम via Prakrit कम्म.

questions.question: संस्कृतस्य 'अक्षि' इत्यस्य हिन्दीभाषायां तद्भवरूपम् ____ इति। (The Hindi tadbhava form of Sanskrit अक्षि is ____.)
questions.explanation: अक्षि → आँख, with क्ष → ख and a candrabindu nasal.

questions.question: भारतीयलिपीनां जननी ____ लिपिः अस्ति। (The mother of the Indian scripts is the ____ script.)
questions.explanation: Almost all Indian scripts descend from Brahmi.

questions.question: संस्कृतस्य हिन्द्याः मराठ्याः च लेखनाय ____ लिपिः प्रयुज्यते। (For writing Sanskrit, Hindi and Marathi the ____ script is used.)
questions.explanation: Devanagari, a daughter of Brahmi, serves Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali.

questions.question: 'Television' इत्यस्य कृते संस्कृतमूलकः पारिभाषिकशब्दः ____ इति। (The Sanskrit-based technical term for 'television' is ____.)
questions.explanation: दूर + दर्शन = seeing from afar.

questions.question: 'University' इत्यस्य कृते संस्कृतमूलकः शब्दः ____ इति। (The Sanskrit-based word for 'university' is ____.)
questions.explanation: विश्व + विद्या + आलय — the abode of universal learning.

questions.question: 'तत्सम' इति शब्दस्य व्युत्पत्तिः — तस्य ____ इति। (The etymology of तत्सम is 'तस्य ____'.)
questions.explanation: तस्य समः — 'same as it (Sanskrit)'.

questions.question: 'तद्भव' इति शब्दस्य व्युत्पत्तिः — तस्मात् ____ इति। (The etymology of तद्भव is 'तस्मात् ____'.)
questions.explanation: तस्मात् भवः — 'born from it (Sanskrit)'.

questions.question: विद्या + आलयः = ____ (दीर्घसन्धिः)। (विद्या + आलयः joins to give ____.)
questions.explanation: आ + आ = आ by dirgha sandhi.

questions.question: सूर्य + उदयः = ____ (गुणसन्धिः)। (सूर्य + उदयः joins to give ____.)
questions.explanation: अ + उ = ओ by guna sandhi.

questions.question: केरलस्य संस्कृत-मलयालम्-मिश्रा साहित्यशैली ____ इति कथ्यते। (Kerala's literary style mixing Sanskrit and Malayalam is called ____.)
questions.explanation: Manipravalam — 'gems and coral'.

questions.question: तमिळभाषायाः प्राचीनं व्याकरणग्रन्थम् ____ इति। (The ancient grammar of the Tamil language is ____.)
questions.explanation: Tolkappiyam, a monument of Tamil's independent classical tradition.

questions.question: 'Radio' इत्यस्य कृते संस्कृतमूलकः शब्दः ____ इति — 'voice from the sky'। (The Sanskrit-based word for 'radio' is ____.)
questions.explanation: आकाश (sky) + वाणी (voice).

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by परस्परसमृद्धिः (mutual enrichment) among Indian languages?
questions.answer: It means the exchange between Sanskrit and the other Indian languages went in both directions: Sanskrit gave vocabulary (tatsama and tadbhava words, technical coinages) to the languages, and they in turn kept Sanskrit alive, carried its ideas to every region, and lent it words of their own. The languages nourish one another like sisters — there is no hierarchy.
questions.explanation: सर्वाः भारतीयाः भाषाः भगिन्यः इव परस्परं पोषयन्ति।

questions.question: Name the two major language families of India and two member languages of each.
questions.answer: The Indo-Aryan family — e.g. Hindi and Bengali (also Marathi, Gujarati, Odia, Punjabi, Assamese) — and the Dravidian family — e.g. Tamil and Telugu (also Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu).
questions.explanation: Indo-Aryan languages descend from Old Indo-Aryan; Dravidian languages form an independent family.

questions.question: Describe the path by which Sanskrit vocabulary became the inherited word-stock of modern languages like Hindi and Marathi.
questions.answer: Old Indo-Aryan (Vedic and classical Sanskrit) evolved into the Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrits, then into Apabhramsha, and from Apabhramsha the modern Indo-Aryan languages took shape around the end of the first millennium CE. Words inherited along this path, changing form at each stage, are the tadbhava vocabulary (e.g. हस्त → हाथ); words later taken directly from Sanskrit unchanged are tatsama.
questions.explanation: संस्कृतात् प्राकृतम्, प्राकृतात् अपभ्रंशः, अपभ्रंशात् आधुनिकाः भाषाः।

questions.question: Define तत्सम and तद्भव words with one Hindi example of each.
questions.answer: A तत्सम word is used in the same form as in Sanskrit — e.g. सूर्य (from सूर्यः). A तद्भव word is born from Sanskrit but changed its form while passing through Prakrit and Apabhramsha — e.g. दूध (from दुग्धम्).
questions.explanation: तस्य समः इति तत्समः; तस्मात् भवः इति तद्भवः।

questions.question: Explain the Sanskrit etymologies of the terms तत्सम and तद्भव, and note the sandhi hidden in तद्भव.
questions.answer: तत्सम = तस्य समः, 'same as it (Sanskrit)' — an unchanged loan. तद्भव = तस्मात् भवः, 'born from it (Sanskrit)' — an inherited, changed form. In तत् + भवः = तद्भवः, the unvoiced त् becomes voiced द् before भ् — an example of consonant (व्यञ्जन) sandhi.
questions.explanation: The very names of the two classes teach both their meaning and a sandhi rule.

questions.question: What are देशज and विदेशज words? Give one example of each from Hindi.
questions.answer: देशज words are born of the local soil, belonging neither to Sanskrit nor to a foreign source — e.g. लोटा (also पगड़ी). विदेशज words are borrowed from foreign languages — e.g. स्कूल from English (also बाज़ार from Persian, क़लम from Arabic).
questions.explanation: A living language welcomes all four classes: तत्सम, तद्भव, देशज, विदेशज.

questions.question: Give the Hindi tadbhava form of each: दुग्धम्, कर्णः, सर्पः, शतम्.
questions.answer: दुग्धम् → दूध; कर्णः → कान; सर्पः → साँप; शतम् → सौ.
questions.explanation: Clusters simplify and nasals often survive as candrabindu (साँप).

questions.question: Give the Sanskrit source word of each Hindi word: आँख, गाँव, सात, चाँद.
questions.answer: आँख ← अक्षि; गाँव ← ग्रामः; सात ← सप्त; चाँद ← चन्द्रः.
questions.explanation: Each is a tadbhava inherited through Prakrit and Apabhramsha.

questions.question: What REGULAR sound changes appear in tadbhava derivations? Illustrate with क्षेत्र → खेत, दुग्ध → दूध and चन्द्र → चाँद.
questions.answer: Three regular changes: (1) conjunct consonants simplify — क्ष becomes ख in क्षेत्र → खेत; (2) clusters reduce with compensating vowel length — ग्ध of दुग्ध simplifies giving दूध with a long ऊ; (3) a lost nasal survives as candrabindu — the न् of चन्द्र remains as the nasalisation in चाँद. Such regular correspondences show the words were organically inherited, not casually borrowed.
questions.explanation: Regularity of sound change is the key evidence of inheritance for linguists.

questions.question: Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to a different language family from Sanskrit. Why, then, do they carry so much Sanskrit vocabulary?
questions.answer: Because of centuries of shared life and scholarship: philosophy, religion, science, law and literature in the south drew deeply on Sanskrit learning, and their classical poets composed under the inspiration of the Sanskrit kavya tradition. Vocabulary flowed with these ideas, so the learned word-stock of Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam became very largely Sanskritic even though the languages themselves are Dravidian in origin.
questions.explanation: Borrowing came through cultural partnership, not descent.

questions.question: What is मणिप्रवालम्? Explain the image contained in its name.
questions.answer: Manipravalam is the celebrated literary style of Kerala in which Sanskrit and Malayalam words are woven together in one composition. The name means 'gems and coral' (मणि + प्रवाल): just as rubies and coral are strung together on one thread to make a single beautiful necklace, the two languages are strung together in one literature.
questions.explanation: The image itself celebrates linguistic partnership.

questions.question: What evidence shows that Tamil has an independent classical tradition of its own?
questions.answer: Tamil possesses an ancient classical literature — the Sangam poems — and an ancient grammar, तोल्काप्पियम् (Tolkappiyam), which arose and flourished on Tamil's own strength, independent of Sanskrit. Tamil also adapted the Sanskrit words it received to its own phonology rather than taking them unchanged, showing the vitality of its independent linguistic genius.
questions.explanation: Tamil is a classical language in its own right; its partnership with Sanskrit was between equals.

questions.question: What is the ब्राह्मी script and where is it most famously seen?
questions.answer: Brahmi is the ancient mother script of India, from which almost all later Indian scripts descend. It is most famously seen in the rock and pillar inscriptions (edicts) of Emperor Ashoka, dating to about the 3rd century BCE.
questions.explanation: From Brahmi evolved Devanagari, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and other scripts.

questions.question: Name four modern Indian scripts that descend from Brahmi, including at least one southern script.
questions.answer: Devanagari, Bengali, Gurmukhi and Telugu (other correct answers: Gujarati, Odia, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil — the last through Tamil-Brahmi).
questions.explanation: Both the northern and the southern scripts are daughters of Brahmi.

questions.question: State the two deep structural features shared by all Brahmi-derived scripts, and explain why a Devanagari reader already understands the 'inner logic' of the Telugu script.
questions.answer: (1) They are abugidas: each consonant letter carries an inherent अ, and other vowels are marked with matras. (2) They arrange the alphabet in the same scientific phonetic order — क ख ग घ ङ ... — inherited from the Sanskrit grammarians' analysis of sounds. A Devanagari reader therefore already knows the system of the Telugu script — its inherent vowel, its matras, its alphabet order — and needs to learn only the letter shapes.
questions.explanation: The shared system, not the shapes, is the real inheritance from Brahmi.

questions.question: Explain the formation and meaning of दूरदर्शनम् and आकाशवाणी.
questions.answer: दूरदर्शनम् = दूर (far) + दर्शनम् (seeing, from the root दृश्) — 'seeing from afar', coined for television. आकाशवाणी = आकाश (sky) + वाणी (voice) — 'voice from the sky', coined for radio. Both are modern technical terms minted from Sanskrit elements and shared across Indian languages.
questions.explanation: Modern coinages are typically transparent Sanskrit compounds.

questions.question: Why is Sanskrit the preferred source for technical coinage across Indian languages? Give two reasons with examples.
questions.answer: (1) Systematic derivation: from a single root, prefixes and suffixes generate whole families of precise, self-explaining words — दृश् (see) yields दर्शनम्, प्रदर्शनम्, दूरदर्शनम्, दर्शकः; गण् (count) yields गणना, गणकः, संगणकः. (2) Shared intelligibility: because every Indian language already carries Sanskrit vocabulary, one coinage such as विश्वविद्यालयः or विद्युत् serves Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Telugu and Kannada alike, knitting the languages together in science, law and administration.
questions.explanation: The धातु-उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय machinery plus the shared word-stock make Sanskrit the common mint.

questions.question: Give the Sanskrit-based coinages for: computer, telephone, university, science.
questions.answer: Computer = संगणकः; telephone = दूरभाषः; university = विश्वविद्यालयः; science = विज्ञानम्.
questions.explanation: All four are shared across many Indian languages.

questions.question: Do the सन्धिविच्छेद and name the sandhi: (a) विद्यालयः (b) सूर्योदयः (c) गणेशः.
questions.answer: (a) विद्यालयः = विद्या + आलयः — दीर्घसन्धिः (आ + आ = आ). (b) सूर्योदयः = सूर्य + उदयः — गुणसन्धिः (अ + उ = ओ). (c) गणेशः = गण + ईशः — गुणसन्धिः (अ + ई = ए).
questions.explanation: Dirgha merges like vowels into one long vowel; guna combines अ with इ/ई or उ/ऊ into ए or ओ.

questions.question: Name the samasa of each with its vigraha: राजपुरुषः, रामलक्ष्मणौ, पीताम्बरः.
questions.answer: राजपुरुषः = राज्ञः पुरुषः (the king's man) — तत्पुरुषः. रामलक्ष्मणौ = रामः च लक्ष्मणः च (Rama and Lakshmana) — द्वन्द्वः. पीताम्बरः = पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः (he whose garment is yellow, i.e. Vishnu) — बहुव्रीहिः.
questions.explanation: Tatpurusha has a case relation, dvandva means 'and', bahuvrihi points to someone outside the compound.

questions.question: A friend says: 'Sanskrit gave everything to the Indian languages and received nothing in return.' Respond with two counter-points from the chapter.
questions.answer: (1) Sanskrit also received: linguists cite words such as मुरजः and कुटी as possible Dravidian contributions absorbed into Sanskrit, so borrowing went both ways. (2) The regional languages preserved and enlivened Sanskrit itself — their saints, poets and scholars carried Sanskrit's ideas to every home, their scripts and scholarship kept the classical language a living presence, and their soil gave it new words and vitality. The relation is mutual enrichment, not one-way giving.
questions.explanation: Both the direction of borrowing and the service of preservation refute the one-way claim.

questions.question: Translate into English: "संस्कृतं ददाति, गृह्णाति च। भारतीयाः भाषाः तस्य कुटुम्बः इव सन्ति।"
questions.answer: "Sanskrit gives, and also receives. The Indian languages are like its family." ददाति = gives; गृह्णाति = takes/receives; कुटुम्बः इव = like a family.
questions.explanation: The sentences summarise the chapter's thesis of two-way exchange within one family.

questions.question: Describe the two major language families of India and Sanskrit's distinct relation to each. Mention the historical stages of the Indo-Aryan line and the correct way to describe the Dravidian partnership.
questions.answer: India's major languages fall into two families. The Indo-Aryan family — Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Odia, Punjabi, Assamese, Nepali, Kashmiri, Sindhi — descends from Old Indo-Aryan, the language of the Vedas and of classical Sanskrit. The descent was gradual: Old Indo-Aryan evolved into the Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrits, the Prakrits into Apabhramsha, and from Apabhramsha the modern languages took shape around the end of the first millennium CE. For these languages Sanskrit is an ancestral source: their inherited (tadbhava) vocabulary evolved from Sanskrit words, and they continually replenish themselves with unchanged (tatsama) Sanskrit borrowings. The Dravidian family — Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu — is an independent family with its own ancient roots; these languages are partners of Sanskrit, not its daughters. Tamil in particular has an independent classical tradition (the Sangam poems, the grammar Tolkappiyam). Yet centuries of shared scholarship, religion and literature created a deep partnership in which enormous Sanskrit vocabulary entered Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, while Sanskrit too absorbed regional words. The right description of the whole picture is परस्परसमृद्धिः — mutual enrichment among sister languages, without hierarchy.
questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish descent (Indo-Aryan) from partnership (Dravidian) and name the Prakrit-Apabhramsha stages.

questions.question: Explain the four classes of vocabulary found in the Indo-Aryan languages — तत्सम, तद्भव, देशज, विदेशज — with their etymologies and at least two examples of each. Why is the tatsama-tadbhava pair called the special bond with Sanskrit?
questions.answer: (1) तत्सम (तस्य समः, 'same as it'): words used unchanged from Sanskrit — सूर्य, अग्नि, पुस्तक, विद्या, कवि. Bengali and Marathi are especially rich in them, and every language's formal register draws on them. (2) तद्भव (तस्मात् भवः, 'born from it'): words inherited from Sanskrit through Prakrit and Apabhramsha with a changed form — हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध, ग्राम → गाँव, कर्म → काम, अक्षि → आँख. (3) देशज ('born of the region'): native words of the local soil — लोटा, पगड़ी. (4) विदेशज ('born abroad'): foreign loans — स्कूल (English), बाज़ार (Persian), क़लम (Arabic). The tatsama-tadbhava pair is the special bond with Sanskrit because both classes flow from Sanskrit itself: tatsamas show the living, continuing borrowing from the classical treasury, while tadbhavas show organic descent — their regular sound changes (क्ष → ख, cluster simplification, candrabindu nasals) prove that the everyday core of these languages was inherited from Sanskrit through an unbroken chain of speech.
questions.explanation: A full answer gives all four classes with etymologies, examples, and the inheritance argument.

questions.question: Using at least six Sanskrit → Hindi pairs from the lesson, analyse the regular sound changes seen in tadbhava words. Why do linguists value such regular correspondences?
questions.answer: Consider: कर्म → काम, हस्तः → हाथ, दुग्धम् → दूध, ग्रामः → गाँव, अक्षि → आँख, चन्द्रः → चाँद, क्षेत्रम् → खेत, सप्त → सात. The changes are regular, not random: (1) conjunct consonants simplify, often with compensating vowel length — प्त of सप्त becomes त in सात, ग्ध of दुग्ध simplifies in दूध, स्त of हस्त in हाथ; (2) the conjunct क्ष regularly becomes ख — क्षेत्र → खेत, अक्षि → आँख; (3) a nasal lost from a cluster survives as candrabindu — चन्द्र → चाँद, ग्राम → गाँव, अक्षि → आँख; (4) internal sounds soften and vowels lengthen — कर्म → (Prakrit कम्म) → काम. Linguists value such regular correspondences because regularity is the signature of inheritance: words that changed by the same phonetic laws must have been passed down through a continuous chain of speakers (Sanskrit → Prakrit → Apabhramsha → Hindi), whereas casual borrowings show no such systematic pattern. The correspondences thus let scholars reconstruct the history of the languages and prove the Indo-Aryan family's descent from Old Indo-Aryan.
questions.explanation: The answer should group examples under stated sound laws and explain the inheritance argument.

questions.question: Write an essay on 'Sanskrit and the Dravidian languages'. Cover the Sanskrit vocabulary of Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, the Manipravalam style, Tamil's classical independence, and the mutual direction of borrowing.
questions.answer: The Dravidian languages — Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam — form an independent family with ancient roots of its own; they are not descendants of Sanskrit. Yet the partnership between Sanskrit and the south is among the richest chapters of India's linguistic history. Telugu and Kannada absorbed a vast Sanskrit vocabulary, above all in philosophy, religion, science, law and literature; their early classical poets composed under the direct inspiration of the Sanskrit kavya tradition, and their learned registers remain deeply Sanskritic today. Malayalam created the celebrated मणिप्रवालम् ('gems and coral') style, in which Sanskrit and Malayalam words are strung on one thread like rubies and coral in a single necklace — a living emblem of partnership between the two literatures. Tamil holds a special place: its Sangam poetry and its ancient grammar तोल्काप्पियम् testify to an independent classical tradition that flourished on its own strength, and Tamil characteristically adapted the Sanskrit words it received to its own phonology rather than taking them unchanged. Nor did the gifts flow one way: linguists cite words such as मुरजः (a drum) and कुटी (hut) as possible Dravidian contributions absorbed by Sanskrit itself. The story of Sanskrit and the Dravidian languages is therefore one of mutual respect and mutual enrichment between great traditions — संस्कृतं ददाति, गृह्णाति च।
questions.explanation: The essay must respect Tamil's independent classical status and present borrowing as two-way.

questions.question: Trace the history of Indian scripts from Brahmi to the modern scripts. Mention Ashoka's inscriptions, Kharoshthi, the major descendant scripts, and the two structural features all Brahmi-born scripts share.
questions.answer: The mother of Indian writing is the ब्राह्मी script, seen most famously in the rock and pillar edicts of Emperor Ashoka, of about the 3rd century BCE. A second ancient script, खरोष्ठी, written from right to left in the north-west, flourished for a time but died out leaving no descendants. From Brahmi, by gradual regional evolution over many centuries, arose nearly all the scripts of India: in the north, Devanagari (used for Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali), the Bengali-Assamese script, Gujarati, Gurmukhi (Punjabi) and Odia; in the south, the Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam scripts, and the Tamil script through the Tamil-Brahmi variety. All these daughters of Brahmi share two deep structural features. First, they are abugidas: every consonant letter carries an inherent अ, and other vowels are indicated by matras attached to the consonant. Second, they arrange their alphabets in the same scientific phonetic order — क ख ग घ ङ, च छ ज झ ञ ... — inherited from the Sanskrit grammarians' analysis of speech sounds by place and manner of articulation. Because the SYSTEM is shared even where the shapes differ, a reader of Devanagari already understands the inner logic of the Telugu or Kannada script. The scripts of India are thus one family — many faces, one mother.
questions.explanation: The answer should cover Brahmi's date and fame, Kharoshthi's extinction, named descendants north and south, and the abugida + phonetic-order features.

questions.question: Analyse Sanskrit's role as the 'shared mint' of modern technical vocabulary. Explain the derivational machinery with the roots दृश् and गण्, give at least six coinages, and state two benefits of this shared coinage for India.
questions.answer: When modern life demanded words for new things, India's languages turned together to Sanskrit, whose derivational machinery — धातु (root) + उपसर्ग (prefix) + प्रत्यय (suffix) — mints precise, transparent terms. From दृश् 'to see' flow दर्शनम् (seeing), प्रदर्शनम् (exhibition), दर्शकः (viewer) and दूरदर्शनम् (television, 'seeing from afar'); from गण् 'to count' flow गणना (counting), गणकः (calculator/reckoner) and संगणकः (computer). Other shared coinages include आकाशवाणी (radio, 'voice from the sky'), दूरभाषः (telephone), विश्वविद्यालयः (university), महाविद्यालयः (college), प्रधानमन्त्री (prime minister), विज्ञानम् (science), प्रौद्योगिकी (technology), विद्युत् (electricity) and शल्यचिकित्सा (surgery). Two benefits follow. First, transparency: because each coinage is built from known roots, its meaning is self-explaining to any speaker who knows the Sanskrit elements — दूरदर्शनम् explains itself as 'far-seeing'. Second, unity: the same coinage serves Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Telugu and Kannada alike, so the vocabulary of law, administration, science and education is shared across the country, knitting the languages together. Sanskrit's coinages even travelled abroad — Indonesian 'bahasa' is भाषा — showing the reach of this shared mint.
questions.explanation: The answer must show the root-derivation families, list coinages, and argue transparency and pan-Indian intelligibility.

questions.question: From the grammar of this lesson: (a) explain दीर्घ, गुण and व्यञ्जन sandhi with one example each; (b) name the four main samasa types with one example each; (c) decline भाषा in the प्रथमा, द्वितीया, तृतीया and सप्तमी singular.
questions.answer: (a) Sandhi. दीर्घसन्धिः: like simple vowels merge into one long vowel — विद्या + आलयः = विद्यालयः (आ + आ = आ); similarly महा + आत्मा = महात्मा. गुणसन्धिः: अ/आ + इ/ई gives ए, and अ/आ + उ/ऊ gives ओ — सूर्य + उदयः = सूर्योदयः; गण + ईशः = गणेशः. व्यञ्जनसन्धिः: a consonant changes before another consonant — तत् + भवः = तद्भवः, where unvoiced त् becomes voiced द् before भ्; likewise वाक् + ईशः = वागीशः. (b) Samasa. तत्पुरुषः: राजपुरुषः = राज्ञः पुरुषः (the king's man). कर्मधारयः: नीलोत्पलम् = नीलम् उत्पलम् (blue lotus). द्वन्द्वः: रामलक्ष्मणौ = रामः च लक्ष्मणः च. बहुव्रीहिः: पीताम्बरः = पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः (he whose garment is yellow — Vishnu). (c) भाषा (feminine आकारान्त), singular: प्रथमा भाषा; द्वितीया भाषाम्; तृतीया भाषया ('by the language'); सप्तमी भाषायाम् ('in the language').
questions.explanation: All examples are drawn from the lesson; modern coinages like दूरदर्शनम् are themselves tatpurusha/karmadharaya compounds.

questions.question: "संस्कृतं भारतीयभाषाणां स्रोतः अपि, सखा अपि" — 'Sanskrit is both a source and a friend of the Indian languages.' Evaluate this statement, weighing evidence for 'source', for 'friend', and against any notion of hierarchy.
questions.answer: As SOURCE: for the Indo-Aryan languages Sanskrit is literally ancestral — their tadbhava core (हस्त → हाथ, दुग्ध → दूध) descended from it through Prakrit and Apabhramsha, and their tatsama vocabulary is drawn from it unchanged. For all languages, including the Dravidian family, Sanskrit is the source of a vast learned vocabulary and of modern technical coinages (दूरदर्शनम्, संगणकः, विश्वविद्यालयः) minted from its roots. Even the scripts descend from one mother, Brahmi, sharing the abugida principle and phonetic order shaped by Sanskrit's grammarians. As FRIEND: Sanskrit did not dominate but partnered — Malayalam's Manipravalam strings Sanskrit and Malayalam like gems and coral; Telugu and Kannada poets drew on the kavya tradition while building great literatures of their own; Tamil kept its independent classical genius while exchanging words with Sanskrit; and Sanskrit itself accepted regional words (मुरज, कुटी are cited as possible Dravidian gifts). AGAINST HIERARCHY: the regional languages preserved and popularised Sanskrit's ideas, kept it a living presence, and enriched it in return; each language, classical or modern, serves its own people fully. The statement is therefore well judged: Sanskrit stands to India's languages as both an ancestral spring and an equal companion — a shared treasury around which sister languages gather, none above the other.
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation cites descent and coinage for 'source', partnership and two-way borrowing for 'friend', and mutual service against hierarchy.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "भारतम् अनेकभाषाभूषितं राष्ट्रम् अस्ति। तासु सर्वासु भाषासु संस्कृतस्य छाया दृश्यते। संस्कृतात् प्राकृतम्, प्राकृतात् अपभ्रंशः, अपभ्रंशात् च आधुनिकाः भाषाः जाताः।" (a) What does 'संस्कृतस्य छाया' mean here? (b) List, in order, the stages named for the birth of the modern languages. (c) Which family of modern languages does this chain of descent describe?
questions.answer: (a) 'The shadow (reflection/influence) of Sanskrit' — Sanskrit's presence is visible in all the languages of India. (b) Sanskrit → Prakrit → Apabhramsha → the modern languages. (c) The Indo-Aryan family (Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Gujarati etc.); the Dravidian languages are related to Sanskrit by partnership, not by this descent.
questions.explanation: The passage states the historical chain of the Indo-Aryan line; छाया is a metaphor for pervasive influence.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "हिन्दीभाषायां चतुर्विधाः शब्दाः सन्ति — तत्समाः, तद्भवाः, देशजाः, विदेशजाश्च। 'सूर्य' इति तत्समः, 'हाथ' इति तद्भवः, 'लोटा' इति देशजः, 'स्कूल' इति विदेशजः।" (a) State the defining feature of each of the four classes. (b) Add one more example of a tatsama and one more of a tadbhava from the lesson.
questions.answer: (a) तत्सम — used in the same form as in Sanskrit; तद्भव — born from Sanskrit but changed in form through Prakrit/Apabhramsha; देशज — native to the local soil, from neither Sanskrit nor abroad; विदेशज — borrowed from a foreign language. (b) Tatsama: अग्नि (or पुस्तक, विद्या, कवि); tadbhava: दूध from दुग्धम् (or काम from कर्म, गाँव from ग्रामः, आँख from अक्षि).
questions.explanation: The passage itself gives one example of each class; the lesson supplies many more.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "बङ्गभाषा मराठीभाषा च तत्समशब्दैः अतीव समृद्धे स्तः। सर्वासां भाषाणां शिष्टप्रयोगे तत्समशब्दाः एव प्रायः प्रयुज्यन्ते।" (a) Which two languages are named as especially rich in tatsama words? (b) In which register (style) of a language are tatsama words mostly used, according to the passage? (c) Why do formal registers prefer tatsama words?
questions.answer: (a) Bengali (बङ्गभाषा) and Marathi (मराठीभाषा). (b) In the formal/literary register (शिष्टप्रयोग). (c) Because tatsama words carry the precision and prestige of the classical Sanskrit treasury, are shared across languages, and suit scholarly, legal and literary usage, while everyday speech leans on tadbhava and deshaja words.
questions.explanation: शिष्टप्रयोगः = cultivated/formal usage; tatsamas are the pan-Indian learned vocabulary.

questions.question: A student prepares this list of Sanskrit → Hindi pairs: (1) कर्म → काम (2) सूर्य → सूर्य (3) क्षेत्रम् → खेत (4) चन्द्रः → चाँद (5) स्कूल → स्कूल. (a) Which pairs show tadbhava derivation? (b) Which entry is tatsama? (c) Which entry does not belong in a Sanskrit-derivation list at all, and why? (d) State the sound change in pair (3).
questions.answer: (a) Pairs 1, 3 and 4 are tadbhava derivations (कर्म → काम, क्षेत्र → खेत, चन्द्र → चाँद). (b) Entry 2, सूर्य, is tatsama — the form is unchanged from Sanskrit. (c) Entry 5, स्कूल, does not belong: it is a विदेशज word borrowed from English 'school', not derived from Sanskrit. (d) In क्षेत्र → खेत the conjunct क्ष regularly becomes ख (with simplification of the cluster त्र to त).
questions.explanation: The exercise tests classification of tatsama, tadbhava and videshaja plus knowledge of the क्ष → ख law.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "केरलदेशे मणिप्रवालम् इति काव्यशैली प्रसिद्धा। यथा मणयः प्रवालाश्च एकस्मिन् सूत्रे ग्रथ्यन्ते, तथा संस्कृतशब्दाः मलयालम्-शब्दाश्च एकस्मिन् काव्ये ग्रथ्यन्ते।" (a) What is compared to gems and coral in this passage? (b) What does the image of 'one thread' (एकं सूत्रम्) signify? (c) What does this style show about the relation between Sanskrit and Malayalam?
questions.answer: (a) Sanskrit words and Malayalam words are compared to gems (मणयः) and coral (प्रवालाः). (b) The single thread signifies one composition/poem in which both languages are woven together as equals, each keeping its own beauty. (c) It shows a relation of partnership and mutual adornment — the two languages enrich one poem together, an emblem of mutual enrichment rather than hierarchy.
questions.explanation: यथा...तथा frames the simile: as a necklace strings gems and coral, so Manipravalam strings the two languages.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "तमिळभाषायाः स्वकीया प्राचीना साहित्यपरम्परा अस्ति — सङ्गमकाव्यानि तोल्काप्पियम् इति व्याकरणं च। तथापि तमिळभाषा अपि संस्कृतशब्दान् स्वीकृत्य स्वरीत्या योजितवती।" (a) What two monuments of Tamil's own tradition are named? (b) What does 'स्वरीत्या योजितवती' tell us about HOW Tamil used Sanskrit words? (c) A classmate concludes 'therefore Tamil depends on Sanskrit'. Assess this conclusion.
questions.answer: (a) The Sangam poems (सङ्गमकाव्यानि) and the ancient grammar Tolkappiyam (तोल्काप्पियम्). (b) It tells us Tamil adopted Sanskrit words 'in its own manner' — adapting them to its own phonology and patterns rather than taking them unchanged. (c) The conclusion is wrong. The passage itself shows Tamil's literature and grammar arose independently; accepting some Sanskrit words is enrichment by contact, which all languages practise, not dependence. Tamil is a classical language in its own right, and the exchange with Sanskrit was a partnership between equals.
questions.explanation: The passage balances Tamil's independence (स्वकीया परम्परा) with its selective, adapted borrowing (स्वरीत्या).

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "अशोकस्य शिलालेखाः ब्राह्मीलिप्यां लिखिताः सन्ति। तस्याः एव लिपेः देवनागरी, बङ्गलिपिः, तेलुगुलिपिः, कन्नडलिपिः, तमिळलिपिश्च क्रमेण जाताः। खरोष्ठी तु लुप्ता अभवत्।" (a) In which script are Ashoka's inscriptions written? (b) Name the five descendant scripts listed. (c) What happened to Kharoshthi? (d) What does this passage prove about the unity of Indian scripts?
questions.answer: (a) In the Brahmi script. (b) Devanagari, the Bengali script, the Telugu script, the Kannada script and the Tamil script. (c) Kharoshthi became extinct (लुप्ता) — it died out leaving no descendants. (d) It proves that the scripts of both north and south India descend from one common mother, Brahmi — the writing systems of India form a single family.
questions.explanation: क्रमेण जाताः = 'arose in due course'; the shared descent underlies the scripts' common abugida system.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "दृश् इति धातोः दर्शनम्, प्रदर्शनम्, दूरदर्शनम्, दर्शकः इति शब्दाः जायन्ते। एवम् एव गण् इति धातोः गणना, गणकः, संगणकः इति। अतः नवीनानां पारिभाषिकशब्दानां निर्माणाय संस्कृतम् एव समर्थम्।" (a) List the four words derived from दृश् and their shared idea. (b) Which modern machine is named by a गण्-derived word, and what does the derivation literally suggest? (c) What conclusion does the passage draw, and give one reason from the lesson supporting it.
questions.answer: (a) दर्शनम् (seeing), प्रदर्शनम् (exhibition/showing forth), दूरदर्शनम् (television, 'seeing from afar'), दर्शकः (viewer) — all share the idea of seeing, from the root दृश्. (b) The computer, named संगणकः — literally 'that which counts/reckons together', from गण् 'to count'. (c) Conclusion: Sanskrit alone is fully capable of generating new technical terms (पारिभाषिकशब्दाः). Supporting reason: its systematic धातु-उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय derivation makes each coinage precise and self-explaining, and because all Indian languages share Sanskrit vocabulary, one coinage is intelligible across the whole country.
questions.explanation: The passage demonstrates root-family derivation, the engine of Sanskrit's modern coinage.

questions.question: Study these formations from the lesson and answer: विद्या + आलयः = विद्यालयः; सूर्य + उदयः = सूर्योदयः; तत् + भवः = तद्भवः; राजपुरुषः = राज्ञः पुरुषः। (a) Name the sandhi in each of the first three formations. (b) Which of the four is a samasa rather than a simple sandhi join, and which samasa type is it? (c) Give the सन्धिविच्छेद of महात्मा.
questions.answer: (a) विद्यालयः — दीर्घसन्धिः (आ + आ = आ); सूर्योदयः — गुणसन्धिः (अ + उ = ओ); तद्भवः — व्यञ्जनसन्धिः (त् → द् before the voiced भ्). (b) राजपुरुषः is a samasa — a तत्पुरुष compound, with the first member in a genitive relation to the second (राज्ञः पुरुषः, 'the king's man'). (c) महात्मा = महा + आत्मा (दीर्घसन्धिः, आ + आ = आ).
questions.explanation: Sandhi joins sounds; samasa joins words into a compound — राजपुरुषः shows both processes at work in word formation.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer: "संस्कृतं ददाति, गृह्णाति च। तत् भारतीयभाषाभ्यः शब्दान् ददाति, ताभ्यश्च नवजीवनं प्राप्नोति। सर्वाः भाषाः भगिन्यः इव परस्परं पोषयन्ति। न कोऽपि उच्चः, न कोऽपि नीचः।" (a) Translate the last sentence. (b) What two-way exchange does the passage describe? (c) Using ONE example each from vocabulary and from scripts, justify the passage's claim of sisterhood among Indian languages.
questions.answer: (a) 'No one is high, no one is low' — there is no hierarchy among the languages. (b) Sanskrit gives words to the Indian languages, and receives new life from them — they preserve it, carry its ideas everywhere, and lend it words in return. (c) Vocabulary: the same Sanskrit treasury serves all — Hindi's tadbhava हाथ (from हस्त) and Telugu's or Malayalam's learned Sanskrit vocabulary show one inheritance shared by both families, while Sanskrit itself absorbed regional words like मुरज and कुटी. Scripts: Devanagari in the north and the Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Tamil scripts in the south all descend from one mother, Brahmi, and share the abugida system and phonetic order — daughters of one house, hence sisters.
questions.explanation: The passage is the chapter's thesis in miniature: mutual giving, mutual receiving, no hierarchy.
